newsitem.title: UK: IPA hits at UK's TV ad inflation, BBC competition.
newsitem.headline: IPA hits at UK's TV ad inflation, BBC competition.

text.p: One of Britain's main advertising trade bodies, the Institute of Practioners in Advertising (IPA), has complained to the government about TV advertising costs and the role of the state-funded British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).
The IPA said on Monday it filed a report in January to Britain's National Heritage Committee that said the skyrocketing cost of television advertising space was hurting the British economy.
It said advertising space on Britain's commercial television had risen by 29 percent since 1992, compared with an increase of 11 percent in the retail price index over the same period.

"This level of increase is showing no signs of abating and the latest figures for the year 1996 show an increase in television advertising costs of eight percent versus an RPI increase of 2.5 percent," the report said.
The IPA said this level of TV advertising inflation was bad for the British economy because British business relied heavily on television as a means of advertising its products.
"It raises the cost of entry for competitors, slows product innovation and tends to force up retail prices to the consumer," said the statement.
The IPA said the inflation of TV advertising space was worse in Britain than in many other major European markets.
It said the situation was exacerbated for advertisers in Britain because the BBC, which runs two of Britain's four main TV channels, did not carry advertising.
"This is very different from other countries in Europe where by far the majority of viewing is accounted for by stations which take advertising," the IPA said.
The IPA said that to curb inflation "more commercial TV channels are needed in order to encourage innovation and to provide competition in the market for television advertising sales".
The IPA represents the majority of the UK advertising industry, which last year handled advertising with an estimated value of 5.75 billion pounds.

It said it was delighted over the imminent arrival of Britain's Channel 5, which is due to be launched in March, but it said it did not expect the new channel to increase overall TV viewing time in Britain.
The IPA said the number of average daily hours of viewing by all individuals in Britain aged four and older had declined steadily to 3.59 hours in 1996 from 3.81 hours in 1992.

It also criticised the BBC for what it described as head-on competition with commercial television to win the "ratings battle" and said the BBC should offer programmes that were unavailable on commerical TV.
"If the BBC follows programme policies designed to maximise ratings, this limits the audiences which ITV and the other commercial broadcasters can reach," the IPA said.
The report said the ITV commercial network saw its share of overall television viewing shrink from 55 percent in the 1970s to 35 percent by 1996, while BBC1 and BBC2 lost much less.

The two BBC channels accounted for 44 percent of total television viewing in 1996, down slightly from 45 percent in the 1970s, while Channel 4 went from nothing to 11 percent and satellite and cable recently grabbed 10 percent of all viewing.
"The IPA is concerned about the consequences of a BBC, supported by the licence fee, allowed in practice to replicate any programming put out by the commercial broadcasters," it said.

"It means the ITV companies in particular, under financial pressures from their franchise commitments and from BBC frontal challenge to their schedules, will not be able to meet their quality obligations and will lose even more viewing share to the BBC," the IPA said.
